name: cpu_hpc_fft

license.notes: Task source stays source-available; PocketFFT is BSD-3-Clause (permissive), so compiling it in imposes no copyleft.

libraries.name: PocketFFT (C++)
libraries.usage: Computes the forward and inverse 3D real FFTs of every solver time step; together with the pointwise passes in between they are the measured workload.
libraries.notes: Header only library compiled into each SIMD tier of the task under its own namespace from the pinned submodule; no source modifications. The same C++ library is the FFT engine of NumPy (numpy.fft since 2.0), SciPy (scipy.fft since 1.4, through its pypocketfft bindings) and PyTorch (CPU FFTs in builds without Intel MKL), so the task runs the code that most Python based scientific work already uses.

title: Scientific fluid simulation
short_description: Double precision spectral fluid simulation across all cores.

structured_text.description: Simulates an incompressible fluid flow in a 3D box with a pseudo-spectral solver, the method used in turbulence research and many physics codes. Every time step runs a series of double precision fast Fourier transforms over a 128 x 128 x 128 grid on all cores. The grid needs around 300 MB of memory, so the test exercises arithmetic, the cache hierarchy and main memory together, just like real simulations.
structured_text.metric_explanation: The score is the number of completed simulation time steps per second, averaged over the run.
structured_text.value_interpretation: Higher is better. More steps per second means larger models and longer simulations finish in reasonable time.
structured_text.reasoning: Fourier transforms on large grids are the building block of spectral solvers, signal processing and many engineering codes. They mix floating point math with strided memory access across all cache levels, so the time step rate predicts real scientific performance better than a peak throughput test. The transforms come from PocketFFT, the open source FFT library behind NumPy, SciPy and the CPU path of PyTorch, so the measured code is the same that runs in everyday scientific and data work.
